opus-5.5.text:
Rainblood was one of those games I stumbled into back when Chinese indie games were still a very small, almost underground scene. It was made with RPG Maker, so on paper it shouldn't have felt that special, but the moment I started playing, the atmosphere just pulled me in.

First, the mood. The world was dark, rainy, and kind of melancholic, a very different take on wuxia from the heroic, colorful martial-arts stories I grew up with. It felt more like a noir film set in the jianghu: everyone carrying secrets, nobody purely good or evil. The art direction and music were restrained, almost cold, and that coldness made the story land harder.

Second, the storytelling. It didn't spoon-feed you. You pieced the plot together through fragments, dialogue, and small details, and there was this sense that the world was much bigger than what you were shown. As a player I found that really respectful. It trusted me to be curious.

Third, it was a statement of possibility. Here was a game made by a tiny team, maybe essentially one person at the start, with limited tools, and it had a distinct voice and aesthetic that felt unmistakably Chinese without being cliché. For me that was eye-opening. It made me think, okay, you don't need a huge studio or a huge budget to make something people remember. You need taste, conviction, and a clear point of view.

So I think what appealed to me wasn't any single mechanic. It was the feeling that someone had poured a very personal vision into it, and you could sense that on every screen. That kind of authorship is rare, and it's something I've kept chasing ever since.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the first thing that got me was that it felt like someone had made it alone, in a room, late at night. Rainblood was this indie wuxia game, pixel art, moody, rain everywhere, and you could feel the person behind it. It wasn't polished the way a big studio title is, and that roughness was the appeal. Every screen felt like a decision one human had made.

The second thing was the atmosphere. Most wuxia stuff I'd grown up with was bright, heroic, lots of flying across rooftops. Rainblood was the opposite. It was slow and wet and a little sad, more noir than martial arts epic. The protagonist, Soul, isn't really a hero. He's tired. The world is tired. And I remember thinking, oh, you can do wuxia this way. You can take the genre and make it quiet.

And then there was just the fact that it existed. At that time, a Chinese indie game with that much personality, made by basically one person, was rare. It made the whole thing feel possible. Like, if he could do that, then the gap between wanting to make something and actually making it wasn't as wide as I'd thought. I think that stayed with me more than any specific scene in the game.
